newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: U.S. Federal Reserve policymakers met on Wednesday to consider interest-rate strategy amid fresh indications of muted inflation that analysts said meant little likelihood of a rate change.
The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee began meeting at 9 a.m. EST (1400 GMT) and a decision was expected around 2:15 p.m. (1915 GMT).

Shortly before the meeting started the Labour Department reported that wholesale prices rose a moderate 0.4 percent in October. Excluding volatile food and energy, however, prices fell 0.3 percent last month, partly because of lower prices for new cars.

"I would expect the Fed to take no action for both the November and December meetings," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "Inflation is not out there with this number."

With inflation seemingly under control and economic growth slowing to a more sustainable pace, analysts almost universally saw little reason for the central bank to alter rates now -- either up or down.
"We don't expect any changes from the Fed," said Barbara Marcin, a vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management. "The economic picture is almost perfectly mixed."
Since trimming short-term rates in January, the Fed has kept policy unchanged as the economy has waxed and waned.
All 37 of Wall Street's premier companies surveyed by Reuters said they expect the central bank to maintain that steady-as-she-goes policy through the end of the year.
It was only seven weeks ago that many of the same firms were betting that the Fed would raise rates to cool off an economy that seemed to be on the verge of over-heating.
But since then economic growth has slowed markedly, to an annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the third quarter from a rapid 4.7 percent pace in the second.
"While growth will pick up in the fourth quarter, it will remain at a subdued pace," said Chris Varvares, president of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers.

The slowdown is welcome news for the Fed because it means the economy is settling down to its long-run cruising speed of between 2 percent and 2.5 percent growth per year -- a rate that could be sustained indefinitely without fanning inflation.

It has also proved to be good news for the financial markets. Stock prices rose to another record on Wednesday and long-term interest rates dropped to their lowest level since March, partly on expectations the Fed will hold policy steady.
The Wall Street rally was also fuelled by hopes that newly re-elected President Bill Clinton will be able to work out a deal with Congress to balance the debt-ridden federal budget.

Analysts were divided over the outlook for Fed policy in the new year. But an overwhelming majority of those polled by Reuters -- 24 of 37 -- expect the central bank's next move to be an increase in rates to keep inflation in check.
At 5.2 percent, the unemployment rate is hovering around a 7-1/2-year low and is at a level that in the past has presaged stepped-up wage demands from workers, and higher inflation.
"The Fed will have to begin tightening by the spring," said James Glassman, an economist at Chemical Securities on Wall Street.
